newsitem.title: USA: Zenith plans to cut work force by 25 percent.
newsitem.headline: Zenith plans to cut work force by 25 percent.

text.p: Zenith Electronics Corp., citing "huge losses," said Wednesday it will cut 1,175 jobs, more than 25 percent of the consumer electronics maker's work force.
Zenith President Peter Willmott said the company plans to eliminate about 375 salaried positions, reducing its U.S. salaried work force to fewer than 1,500.

The Glenview, Ill.-based company said it will cut about 800 hourly positions, largely through attrition, at its Melrose Park, Ill., colour picture tube plant as new automated processes improve productivity.
This will reduce Zenith's total U.S. hourly work force to about 2,000.
"Our fixed costs are simply too high for a company with sales at our levels and reporting such huge losses," Willmott said in a letter to employees.
He called the company's plans "a necessary step in Zenith's turnaround process."
However, industry analysts questioned whether the moves were enough, and cautioned that they might hinder the company's turnaround effort.
The job cuts are expected to reduce expenses by about $20 million in 1997 and result in a fourth-quarter restructuring charge of about $25 million, Zenith said.
"Whether the expected $20 million is enough is a question," said Duff & Phelps analyst George Podrasky.
"It looks like a neutron bomb went off at headquarters at the moment," said Robert Gutenstein of Kalb Voohris & Co.
He added, "It raises the questions 'Is it enough?' or 'Will they scare out peple who are part of the solution rather than the problem?'"
In October, Zenith reported net losses of $109 million for the first nine months of 1996.
The company said it was in discussions with its lenders and expected to amend some financial covenants in its lending agreement.

In its latest filing with the Securities Exchange Commission, Zenith reported that its financial covenants require the company to have a net worth equal to or greater than $211 million. As of Sept. 28, 1996, Zenith said its net worth was $220.3 million.

"They were close (to the limit)," said Podrasky, noting that in his view Zenith will continue to require funds from LG Electronics Inc., the South Korean company that owns 55 percent of Zenith's outstanding shares.
The Korean company, known in part for its GoldStar electronics products, makes semiconductors as well as automobile parts.

In its filing, cash-strapped Zenith also said it temporarily delayed construction activities at a planned large-screen picture tube manufacturing plant in Woodridge, Ill., as it "explores a range of financing alternatives and studies industry dynamics."
Zenith's stock lost $1.50 to $10.875 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
